idiom_name: enum Message + switch (with @unknown default for non-frozen cases) + [String: (Message) -> Void] registry
implementation_notes: The idiomatic Swift router combines a closed part and an open part: the message shape is an enum switched exhaustively (the compiler rejects a switch that misses a case, and @unknown default keeps a switch over a non-frozen imported enum future-compatible), while the runtime-editable part is a dictionary of handlers republished as a whole behind a lock or a serial DispatchQueue so each message takes one immutable snapshot. Concurrency checking is satisfied either by confining the registry to an actor or by marking the published value Sendable. Keeping the rules in a registry rather than in the switch is exactly what lets destinations change without a rebuild; use the switch alone when the mapping is fixed.
pitfalls: Closures in the registry capture their context: a strong capture of a destination keeps it alive after its rule is retired (a classic leak) - capture weakly or clear the registry on republish.
Reading and writing the registry without the lock is a data race that Swift 6 strict concurrency diagnoses for Sendable values; use an actor or one explicit lock consistently.

Exhaustive switches over a non-frozen imported enum need @unknown default or they trap at runtime when the framework adds a case, while using @unknown default on an app-internal enum discards a real compile-time guarantee.

variants.name: Vapor route registration on the RoutingKit trie
variants.idiom_name: Vapor app.get/app.on route registration with PathComponent patterns
variants.implementation_notes: Where the messages arrive as HTTP requests, Vapor's router (the RoutingKit trie) is the router: routes are registered with app.get/app.post/app.on and a variadic list of PathComponent values - constants, :parameters, anything (*) and catchall (**) - and a control channel that registers routes while the server runs changes the route set without a redeploy, with req.parameters exposing the matched components to the handler. Matching is method-and-path based and independent of route count, so this realization suits request-shaped traffic; content-based rules still belong in the handler.
pitfalls: RoutingKit's trie is not documented as safe for concurrent registration, so rule pushes must be serialized (for example on the application's event loop) rather than issued from many tasks.
Path parameter names are looked up by string at runtime, so a typo yields nil instead of a compile error - keep parameter names constants.
Case-insensitive routing is off by default and must be configured before startup, so a rule set that assumes case-insensitive paths quietly returns 404.
